title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: GAR physical faculty vs user; PLAC only mind tip
pass_a_gloss: GAR adds: a last end properly belongs to those who can know the distinction of subaltern ends and the last—which fits neither universal corruption nor a merely physical generative faculty. Better distinguish the faculty from the man who uses it: he can set a last end by intellect and will, but the physical faculty keeps the end Nature's Author fixed—concoction, generation, and so on—whatever the corrupt man attempts. Placeus: if that reasoning holds, only the mind acts for an end, not the will, which does not properly know, much less know last versus subordinate ends. Tip into the fuller reply on faculties and false ends, where pleasure versus generation is pressed harder.
pass_b_english: GAR. Further, since a last end has relation to intermediate and subaltern ends, properly that will be a last end for those who can know the distinction of subaltern ends and the last: which, since it can fit neither that universal corruption nor the generative faculty or any other simply physical one, how will the generative faculty be said to be turned by corruption to generation as to a last end? Distinguishing rather between the faculty and the man who uses the faculty would have been better. For he can indeed by his understanding and will set himself a last end: but the physical faculty itself has the end to which it was determined by the Author of nature, which it always regards, whatever the corrupt man attempts—as the concoctive concoction, the generative generation, &c. PLAC. If the learned man reasons well, only the mind acts for an end, not the will: for the will does not properly know, much less know the distinction between the last end and the subordinate ones.
source_text: GAR. Praeterea, Cum finis ultimus relationem habeat ad fines intermedios & subalternos, eorum erit proprie finis ultimus, qui finium subalternorum, & ultimi distinctionem nosse possunt: quod cum neque in corruptionem universalem illam, neque in facultatem generatricem, aut aliam simpliciter physicam convenire possit, quomodo dicetur facultas genitrix a corruptione converti ad generationem tanquam ad finem ultimum? Distinguendum potius fuerit inter facultatem, & hominem, qui facultate utitur. Hic enim poterit sane intelligentia ac voluntate sua finem ultimum sibi praestituere: sed ipsa facultas physica, finem habet ad quem ab Autore naturae determinata est, quem semper respicit, quicquid homo corruptus moliatur, ut concoctrix concoctionem, genitrix generationem, &c. PLAC. Si bene ratiocinatur vir doctus sola mens agit propter finem, non voluntas: haec enim non cognoscit proprie, nedum ut distinctionem cognoscat inter finem ultimum & subordinatos.
